teaching_card.title: Logarithms (Medium)
teaching_card.body: A logarithm is an exponent: log_b(x) answers 'b to what power gives x?' So log_b(x) = y means exactly b^y = x. Switch between the two forms to solve, and use the product, quotient, and power rules to combine or expand logs.
key_points: log_b(1) = 0, log_b(b) = 1, and b^(log_b x) = x.
log(pq) = log p + log q; log(p/q) = log p − log q; log(p^k) = k·log p.
Solve b^x = c by rewriting both sides with the same base, or x = log c / log b.

screens.title: A log is an exponent
screens.body: Read log₃(81) as 'what power of 3 is 81?' — the answer is 4. Negative results come from fractions (log₂(1/8) = −3) and fractional results from roots (log₉(3) = 1/2). The base 10 is written log x; the base e is ln x.
key_points: Ask: base to what power equals the argument?
Fractions give negative logs; roots give fractional logs.
log₁₀ is written log; logₑ is ln.

screens.title: Switching forms
screens.body: The exponential form b^y = x and the logarithmic form log_b(x) = y say the same thing. The base of the power is the base of the log, the exponent is the value of the log, and the result of the power is the argument. To solve log_b(x + c) = k, rewrite as x + c = b^k.
key_points: Base stays the base; exponent ↔ log value.

screens.title: Log rules
screens.body: Because logs are exponents, multiplying arguments adds logs, dividing subtracts them, and a power inside becomes a multiplier outside: log(x³/y) = 3·log x − log y. Running the rules backward condenses a sum of logs into a single log, which is how you solve log equations.
key_points: Product → sum, quotient → difference, power → coefficient.
Condense before solving: log_b(A) = log_b(B) ⇒ A = B.

screens.title: Try the moves
screens.body: Solve 8^x = 32: both are powers of 2, so 2^(3x) = 2⁵ and x = 5/3. Solve log₅(2x − 1) = 2: 2x − 1 = 25, x = 13. Solve 3^x = 20: x = log 20 / log 3 ≈ 2.73.
